RELIGION AND NATIONAL VALUES
FIRST TERM
WEEK 3
PRIMARY 6
THEME - THE PAUL’S APOSTLE
PREVIOUS LESSON - The Paul’s Conversion - Paul’s Proposed Journey to Damascus Primary 6 (Basic 6) - Christian Religious Studies
TOPIC: PAUL’S CONVERSION
LEARNING AREA
1. Introduction
2. Paul’s Conversion Baptism and Mission
3. Importance of Conversion
4. Lesson Evaluation and Weekly Assessment
PERFORMANCE OBJECTIVES
By the end of the lesson, most of the pupils should have attained the following objectives -
1. explain the baptism and mission of Paul.
2. explain the importance of Paul’s conversion.
ENTRY BEHAVIOR
The pupils can the story of how God arrest Paul on the way to Damascus.
INSTRUCTIONAL MATERIALS
The teacher will teach the lesson with the aid of Bible story books.
METHOD OF TEACHING
Choose a suitable and appropriate methods for the lessons.
Note - Irrespective of choosing methods of teaching, always introduce an activities that will arouse pupil’s interest or lead them to the lessons.
REFERENCE MATERIALS
Scheme of Work
9 - Years Basic Education Curriculum
Living as God’s Children Book 6
All Relevant Materials
Online Information
CONTENT OF THE LESSON
LESSON 1 - INTRODUCTION
Conversion means changing one religion (faith) for another.
PAUL’S CONVERSION, BAPTIST AND MISSION - ACTS 9:10 - 19
For three days, Paul was in Damascus without eating, but praying all the time. Paul saw Jesus sending somebody to him see again, and to baptize.
Jesus appeared to Ananias, one of the Christians in Damascus, He said,”For he (Paul) is a chosen instrument of mine to carry my name before the Gentiles and Kings and sons of Israel.”
Jesus told him to go and help Paul regain his sight, and baptism. He laid his hand on Paul, and he regained his sight. He baptized Paul and became a Christian.
He then received the Holy Spirit. He took some food and was strong again and he began to proclaim that Jesus is Christ.
LESSON 2 - IMPORTANCE OF PAUL’S CONVERSION - ACTS 9:31
31 Then the church throughout Judea, Galilee and Samaria enjoyed a time of peace and was strengthened. Living in the fear of the Lord and encouraged by the Holy Spirit, it increased in numbers.
Importance of Paul’s conversion is to spread Christianity to Gentiles nations.
PRESENTATION
To deliver the lesson, the teacher adopts the following steps:
1. To introduce the lesson, the teacher revises the previous lesson. Based on this, he/she asks the pupils some questions;
2. Explain Paul’s conversion baptism and mission.
3. Leads a discussion on the importance of Paul’s conversion.
4. Summarizes the lesson on the board.
Pupil’s Activities - Copy the notes as instructed.
CONCLUSION
To conclude the lesson for the week, the teacher revises the entire lesson and links it to the following week’s lesson.
NEXT LESSON
Paul’s Mission I - Paul and Barnabas were selected by the Holy Spirit - Paul Preaches to Different People (Primary 6)

topics.title: Paul’s Mission II Primary 6 (Basic 6) - Christian Religious Studies
topics.content:
CHRISTIAN RELIGIOUS STUDIES
RELIGION AND NATIONAL VALUES
FIRST TERM
WEEK 5
PRIMARY 6
THEME - PAUL THE APOSTLE
PREVIOUS LESSON - Paul’s Mission I - Paul and Barnabas were selected by the Holy Spirit - Paul Preaches to Different People Primary 6 (Basic 6) - Christian Religious Studies
TOPIC: PAUL PREACHES TO DIFFERENT PEOPLE
LEARNING AREA
1. Introduction
2. Paul preached to the Jews and Gentiles
3. Paul preached to all Nations in his Community
4. Importance of Missionary Work
4. Lesson Evaluation and Weekly Assessment
PERFORMANCE OBJECTIVES
By the end of the lesson, most of the pupils should have attained the following objectives -
1. name the two major groups of people to whom Paul preached;
2. discuss the importance of missionary work.
ENTRY BEHAVIOR
The pupils can summarize the story of Paul.
INSTRUCTIONAL MATERIALS
The teacher will teach the lesson with the aid of:
1. A map showing St. Paul’s missionary journeys.
2. Illustrations of a church and missionaries preaching before a congregation.
METHOD OF TEACHING
Choose a suitable and appropriate methods for the lessons.
Note - Irrespective of choosing methods of teaching, always introduce an activities that will arouse pupil’s interest or lead them to the lessons.
REFERENCE MATERIALS
Scheme of Work
9 - Years Basic Education Curriculum
Good News Bible
Living as God’s Children Book 6
All Relevant Materials
CONTENT OF THE LESSON
INTRODUCTION
Missionary work is the act of doing the work of faith in Christ Jesus.
It is a command of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ.
John 9:4, I must work the works of him that sent me, while it is day: the night cometh, when no man can work.
Mathew 28:8, Go therefore and make disciples of all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit.
PAUL PREACHED TO THE JEWS AND GENTILES - Acts 18:4-8
Bible reading - Acts 18:4 - 8
4 Every Sabbath he reasoned in the synagogue, trying to persuade Jews and Greeks.
5 When Silas and Timothy came from Macedonia, Paul devoted himself exclusively to preaching, testifying to the Jews that Jesus was the Messiah.
6 But when they opposed Paul and became abusive, he shook out his clothes in protest and said to them, “Your blood be on your own heads! I am innocent of it. From now on I will go to the Gentiles.”
7 Then Paul left the synagogue and went next door to the house of Titius Justus, a worshiper of God.
8 Crispus, the synagogue leader, and his entire household believed in the Lord; and many of the Corinthians who heard Paul believed and were baptized.
PAUL’S PREACHED TO ALL NATIONS IN HIS COMMUNITY - Acts 18:11-18
Bible reading - Acts 18:11 - 18
11 So Paul stayed there for a year and a half, teaching the people the word of God.
12 When Gallio was made the Roman governor of Achaia, Jews there got together, seized Paul, and took him into court. 13 “This man,” they said, “is trying to persuade people to worship God in a way that is against the law!”
14 Paul was about to speak when Gallio said to the Jews, “If this were a matter of some evil crime or wrong that has been committed, it would be reasonable for me to be patient with you Jews.
15 But since it is an argument about words and names and your own law, you yourselves must settle it. I will not be the judge of such things!”
16 And he drove them out of the court.
17 They all grabbed Sosthenes, the leader of the synagogue, and beat him in front of the court. But that did not bother Gallio a bit.
IMPORTANCE OF MISSIONARY WORK
The importance of Missionary work are -
1. Preaching the gospel to people everywhere.
2. Converting people to Christ.
3. Baptist them.
MORAL LESSON
1. God wants us to preach the name of Jesus, like Paul and Barnabas did.
2. God want us to help missionaries establish Church everywhere like Paul and Barnabas did.
PRESENTATION
To deliver the lesson, the teacher adopts the following steps:
1. To introduce the lesson, the teacher revises the previous lesson. Based on this, he/she asks the pupils some questions;
2. Discusses Paul’s messages to the Jews and Gentiles.
Pupil’s Activities - Participate in the class discussion.
3. Discusses the importance of missionary work;
Pupil’s Activities - Discuss the importance of missionary work.
4. Lesson summary on the board;
Pupil’s Activities - Note taking.
5. Summarizes each lesson on the board.
Pupil’s Activities - Write as instructed.
CONCLUSION
- To conclude the lesson for the week, the teacher revises the entire lesson and links it to the following week’s lesson.
- Next Lesson - Paul in Europe I - Paul’s Journey from Troas to Macedonia (Primary 6)
LESSON EVALUATION
Ask pupils to:
1. Name 2 major groups to whom Paul preached.
2. Discuss the importance of missionary works.

topics.title: Paul’s Conversion: Meaning of Conversion, Reasons for Paul’s Mission, and His Experience on the Way to Damascus | Primary 6 (Basic 6) First Term Week 2 Christian Religious Studies
topics.content:
PAUL’S CONVERSION: MEANING OF CONVERSION, REASONS FOR PAUL’S MISSION AND HIS EXPERIENCE ON THE WAY TO DAMASCUS
CHRISTIAN RELIGIOUS STUDIES (CRS)
PRIMARY 6 - FIRST TERM - WEEK 2
THEME - NATIONAL RELIGIOUS STUDIES
PREVIOUS LESSON - Paul’s Early Life: Paul’s Parentage and Education, and His Anti-Christian Activities | Primary 6 (Basic 6) First Term Week 1 Christian Religious Studies
TOPIC - PAUL’S CONVERSION
LEARNING AREA
1. Introduction
2. Meaning of Conversion and Paul’s Experience on the Way to Damascus
3. Paul’s Conversion and Response to Jesus
4. Reasons for Paul’s Mission
5. Lessons from Paul’s Conversion
6. Weekly Assessment: Test Questions and Answers/Assignment
7. Summary
LEARNING OBJECTIVES
By the end of the lesson, pupils should be able to:
1. Explain the meaning of conversion.
2. Describe Paul’s experience on the way to Damascus.
3. Explain how Paul was converted.
4. State reasons for Paul’s mission.
5. State lessons from Paul’s conversion.
ENTRY BEHAVIOUR
Pupils have learned about Paul’s early life, education and anti-Christian activities.
This lesson builds on that knowledge by introducing pupils to Paul’s conversion and his new life as a follower and missionary of Jesus Christ.
INSTRUCTIONAL MATERIALS
The teacher will teach the lesson with the aid of:
1. Holy Bible and story illustrations
2. Pictures of Paul
3. Map showing Jerusalem and Damascus
4. Charts
5. Flashcards
METHOD OF TEACHING
Choose a suitable and appropriate methods for the lessons.
Note - Irrespective of choosing methods of teaching, always introduce an activities that will arouse pupil’s interest or lead them to the lessons.
REFERENCE MATERIALS
1. Scheme of Work
2. 9-Year Basic Education Curriculum
3. CRS Course Book
4. Holy Bible - Acts 9:1-19; Acts 22:6-16; Acts 26:12-18
5. Relevant teaching materials
6. Online information
CONTENT OF THE LESSON
INTRODUCTION
Paul was originally called Saul. Before his conversion, he strongly opposed Christians and tried to stop the spread of Christianity.
Paul was travelling to Damascus to arrest Christians when he had a remarkable encounter with Jesus Christ. This experience changed his life completely. He became a follower and missionary of Jesus Christ.
LESSON 1 - MEANING OF CONVERSION
Conversion means a change from one way of life, belief or behaviour to another.
In Christianity, conversion means turning away from sin and accepting Jesus Christ as Lord and Saviour.
Paul’s conversion was a great change in his life. He changed from a persecutor of Christians to a follower, preacher and missionary of Jesus Christ.
PAUL’S EXPERIENCE ON THE WAY TO DAMASCUS
Paul was travelling to Damascus with authority to arrest Christians and take them to Jerusalem.
As he came near Damascus, a bright light from heaven suddenly shone around him. Paul fell to the ground and heard a voice saying, “Saul, Saul, why do you persecute me?”
Paul asked who was speaking. The voice replied that it was Jesus whom Paul was persecuting.
Jesus told Paul to enter Damascus, where he would be told what to do.
Paul got up from the ground but discovered that he could not see. His companions led him by the hand into Damascus.
Paul remained blind for three days. During this period, he neither ate nor drank.
LESSON 2 - PAUL’S CONVERSION AND RESPONSE TO JESUS
God sent a disciple named Ananias to Paul in Damascus. Ananias prayed for him, and Paul regained his sight.
Paul was then baptised and began his new life as a follower of Jesus Christ.
After his conversion, Paul no longer persecuted Christians. Instead, he began preaching that Jesus Christ is the Son of God and Saviour.
His conversion became a turning point in his life.
LESSON 3 - REASONS FOR PAUL’S MISSION
After his conversion, Paul became a missionary of Jesus Christ. His mission was to:
1. Preach the Gospel of Jesus Christ.
2. Tell people about salvation through Jesus Christ.
3. Teach Jews and Gentiles about Christ.
4. Encourage Christians to remain faithful.
5. Establish and strengthen Christian communities.
6. Help people turn away from sin and follow God.
7. Spread the message of Jesus Christ to many places.
LESSONS FROM PAUL’S CONVERSION
Paul’s conversion teaches us that:
1. People can change from bad behaviour to good behaviour.
2. God can give a person a new purpose in life.
3. We should obey God when He calls us to do what is right.
4. We should not persecute or hate others.
5. We should seek the truth before judging others.
6. Our education and abilities should be used for good purposes.
7. We should be willing to serve God and help others.
WEEKLY ASSESSMENT: TEST QUESTIONS AND ANSWERS/ASSIGNMENT
A. Multiple Choice Questions
1. What does conversion mean?
A. Becoming a soldier
B. Travelling to another city
C. Learning a new language
D. Changing from one way of life to another
2. Where was Paul travelling when Jesus appeared to him?
A. Bethlehem
B. Damascus
C. Nazareth
D. Jericho
3. What appeared around Paul on the way to Damascus?
A. A bright light from heaven
B. A heavy rain
C. A large fire
D. A dark cloud
4. Who spoke to Paul on the way to Damascus?
A. Peter
B. Gamaliel
C. Jesus Christ
D. Stephen
5. What did Paul do after his conversion?
A. He continued persecuting Christians
B. He stopped believing in God
C. He became a missionary of Jesus Christ
D. He became a Roman soldier
B. Fill in the Gaps
6. Paul was travelling to ______ when Jesus appeared to him.
7. A bright ______ from heaven shone around Paul.
8. Paul remained blind for ______ days.
9. ______ was sent to Paul in Damascus.
10. Paul was later ______ as a follower of Jesus Christ.
C. True or False
11. Jesus was travelling to Damascus to arrest Christians.
12. Paul heard the voice of David on the way to Jerusalem.
13. Paul continued persecuting Christians before his conversion.
14. Ananias helped Paul regain his sight.
15. Jesus became a preacher of Paul after his conversion.
D. Matching
16. Conversion - A. Helped Paul regain his sight
17. Damascus - B. Paul’s missionary work
18. Jesus Christ - C. Change of life or belief
19. Ananias - D. Place Paul was travelling to
20. Paul’s mission - E. Spoke to Paul on the road
ANSWER KEY
1. D 2. B 3. A 4. C 5. C
6. Damascus. 7. light 8. three 9. Ananias 10. baptised
11. False 12. Fasle 13. True 14. True 15. Fasle
16. C 17. D 18. E 19. A 20. B
SUMMARY
Pupils learned that conversion means a change from one way of life, belief or behaviour to another. Paul experienced a remarkable conversion when Jesus appeared to him on the way to Damascus.
Pupils also learned that Paul changed from a persecutor of Christians to a follower and missionary of Jesus Christ. He preached the Gospel, taught people about Jesus and helped spread Christianity.
PRESENTATION
To deliver the lesson, the teacher adopts the following steps:
Step 1: Introduction
The teacher asks pupils:
- What did Paul do to Christians before his conversion?
- Can a person change from doing wrong to doing good?
- What do you think happened to Paul on his way to Damascus?
The teacher explains that Paul experienced a great change in his life when he encountered Jesus Christ.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils answer the questions and share what they know about Paul.
Step 2: Meaning of Conversion
The teacher explains that conversion means a change from one way of life, belief or behaviour to another. The teacher also explains that Paul changed from a persecutor of Christians to a follower and preacher of Jesus Christ.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils listen and explain the meaning of conversion in their own words.
Step 3: Paul’s Experience on the Way to Damascus
The teacher explains that Paul was travelling to Damascus to arrest Christians. A bright light from heaven appeared around him, and he fell to the ground and heard the voice of Jesus.
The teacher also uses a map to show the journey towards Damascus.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils observe the map, listen to the story and mention what happened to Paul.
Step 4: Paul’s Conversion
The teacher explains that Paul became blind after the encounter with Jesus and was led into Damascus. The teacher explains how Ananias was sent to Paul, prayed for him and helped him regain his sight.
The teacher also explains that Paul was baptised and began a new life as a follower of Jesus Christ.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils describe how Paul’s life changed after his encounter with Jesus.
Step 5: Reasons for Paul’s Mission
The teacher explains that after his conversion, Paul became a missionary of Jesus Christ. He preached the Gospel, taught Jews and Gentiles, encouraged Christians and helped spread Christianity.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils mention some reasons for Paul’s mission.
Step 6: Lessons from Paul’s Conversion
The teacher explains that Paul’s conversion teaches us that people can change, God can give people a new purpose, and our abilities should be used for good.
The teacher also explains that Christians should avoid persecuting others and should be willing to serve God.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils state lessons they have learned from Paul’s conversion.
Step 7: Group Activity
The teacher divides pupils into four groups:
- Group 1: Explain the meaning of conversion and give one example.
- Group 2: Mention five things that happened to Paul on the way to Damascus.
- Group 3: Mention five reasons for Paul’s mission after his conversion.
- Group 4: State four lessons from Paul’s conversion.
The teacher guides the groups and allows each group to present its answers.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils discuss, write and present their answers to the class.
Step 8: Lesson Summary and Evaluation
The teacher reviews the meaning of conversion, Paul’s experience on the way to Damascus, his conversion and reasons for his mission. The teacher gives pupils a different set of 20 questions to assess their understanding of the lesson.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils answer the questions individually or in groups and summarise what they have learned.
CONCLUSION
To conclude the lesson for the week, the teacher revises the entire lesson and links it to the following week’s lesson.
NEXT LESSON
Israel in Bondage: Meaning and Suffering of Bondage, Israel’s Bondage in Egypt, and the Birth of Moses | Primary 6 (Basic 6) First Term Week 3 Christian Religious Studies
LESSON EVALUATION
Teacher asks pupils,
1. What is conversion?
2. What happened to Paul on the way to Damascus?
3. Who helped Paul regain his sight?
4. Mention four reasons for Paul’s mission.
5. State four lessons from Paul’s conversion.

topics.title: The Crossing of the Red Sea: Meaning and Story of the Crossing, and the Destruction of the Egyptians | Primary 6 (Basic 6) First Term Week 5 Christian Religious Studies
topics.content:
THE CROSSING OF THE RED SEA: MEANING AND STORY OF THE CROSSING, AND THE DESTRUCTION OF THE EGYPTIANS
CHRISTIAN RELIGIOUS STUDIES (CRS)
PRIMARY 6 - FIRST TERM - WEEK 5
THEME - NATIONAL RELIGIOUS STUDIES
PREVIOUS LESSON - The Call of Moses: Meaning of Call, The Call of Moses, and Miracles Performed by Moses in Egypt | Primary 6 (Basic 6) First Term Week 4 Christian Religious Studies
TOPIC - THE CROSSING OF THE RED SEA
LEARNING AREA
1. Introduction
2. Meaning of the Crossing of the Red Sea
3. The Story of the Crossing of the Red Sea
4. The Destruction of the Egyptians
5. Lessons from the Crossing of the Red Sea
6. Weekly Assessment: Test Questions and Answers/Assignment
7. Summary
LEARNING OBJECTIVES
By the end of the lesson, pupils should be able to:
1. Explain the meaning of the crossing of the Red Sea.
2. Narrate the story of the Israelites’ crossing of the Red Sea.
3. Explain how God helped the Israelites cross the sea.
4. Describe what happened to the Egyptian army.
5. State lessons from the crossing of the Red Sea.
ENTRY BEHAVIOUR
Pupils have learned about Moses’ call and how God used him to lead the Israelites out of Egypt.
This lesson builds on that knowledge by teaching pupils how God delivered the Israelites from the Egyptian army at the Red Sea.
INSTRUCTIONAL MATERIALS
The teacher will teach the lesson with the aid of:
1. Holy Bible and story illustrations
2. Pictures of Moses and the Israelites crossing the Red Sea
3. Map showing Egypt and the Red Sea
4. Charts
5. Flashcards
METHOD OF TEACHING
Choose a suitable and appropriate methods for the lessons.
Note - Irrespective of choosing methods of teaching, always introduce an activities that will arouse pupil’s interest or lead them to the lessons.
REFERENCE MATERIALS
1. Scheme of Work
2. 9-Year Basic Education Curriculum
3. CRS Course Book
4. Holy Bible - Exodus 14:1-31
5. Relevant teaching materials
6. Online information
CONTENT OF THE LESSON
INTRODUCTION
After Pharaoh finally allowed the Israelites to leave Egypt, Moses led them towards the Promised Land. God guided them on their journey.
When Pharaoh realised that the Israelites had left, he changed his mind and sent his army and chariots after them. The Israelites reached the Red Sea and found themselves trapped between the sea and the approaching Egyptian army.
God then performed a great miracle through Moses and made a way for the Israelites to cross the sea on dry ground.
LESSON 1 - MEANING OF THE CROSSING OF THE RED SEA
The crossing of the Red Sea refers to the event in which God miraculously made a path through the Red Sea for the Israelites to escape from the Egyptian army.
The event showed God’s power and His ability to save His people from danger.
THE STORY OF THE CROSSING OF THE RED SEA
The Israelites left Egypt under the leadership of Moses.
Pharaoh later changed his mind and sent his army, horses and chariots to bring the Israelites back.
When the Israelites saw the Egyptian army approaching, they became afraid and cried to Moses.
Moses told them not to be afraid and to trust God.
God instructed Moses to raise his staff and stretch his hand over the sea. A strong east wind blew throughout the night, and the waters were divided.
The Israelites crossed the Red Sea on dry ground, with the water forming walls on both sides.
The Israelites continued crossing until they reached the other side safely.
LESSON 2 - THE DESTRUCTION OF THE EGYPTIANS
The Egyptian army followed the Israelites into the sea.
After the Israelites had safely crossed, God instructed Moses to stretch his hand over the sea again.
The waters returned to their normal position and covered the Egyptian army, including the horses and chariots.
The Egyptian army was destroyed, while the Israelites escaped safely.
When the Israelites saw what God had done, they feared and trusted God and His servant Moses.
LESSON 3 - LESSONS FROM THE CROSSING OF THE RED SEA
The crossing of the Red Sea teaches us that:
1. We should trust God in difficult situations.
2. God can save people from danger.
3. We should obey God’s instructions.
4. We should not allow fear to overcome our faith.
5. God can make a way when there seems to be no way.
6. Leaders should guide people with courage and faith.
7. We should be grateful when God helps us.
WEEKLY ASSESSMENT: TEST QUESTIONS AND ANSWERS/ASSIGNMENT
A. Multiple Choice Questions
1. Who led the Israelites out of Egypt?
A. Joshua
B. Aaron
C. Moses
D. Joseph
2. What did the Israelites face when they reached the Red Sea?
A. A mountain
B. The Egyptian army behind them
C. A group of traders
D. A large city
3. What did Moses stretch over the sea?
A. His staff
B. His cloak
C. A rope
D. A branch
4. What happened to the waters of the Red Sea?
A. They disappeared forever
B. They became ice
C. They became muddy
D. They were divided so the Israelites could cross
5. What happened to the Egyptian army?
A. They escaped into the desert
B. They returned to Egypt safely
C. They were covered by the returning waters
D. They crossed before the Israelites
B. Fill in the Gaps
6. Moses led the Israelites out of ______.
7. The Israelites crossed the ______ Sea.
8. Moses stretched his ______ over the sea.
9. The Israelites crossed the sea on ______ ground.
10. The Egyptian army was covered by the returning ______.
C. True or False
11. Pharaoh sent his army after the Israelites.
12. The Israelites were afraid when they saw the Egyptian army.
13. Moses told the Israelites to give up and return to Egypt.
14. The Israelites crossed the Red Sea on dry ground.
15. The Egyptian army was destroyed when the waters returned.
D. Matching
16. Moses - A. Covered the Egyptian army
17. Red Sea - B. Led the Israelites
18. Pharaoh - C. Sea crossed by the Israelites
19. Dry ground - D. King of Egypt
20. Egyptian army - E. Path used by the Israelites to cross
ANSWER KEY
1. C 2. B 3. A 4. D 5. C
6. Egypt 7. Red 8. staff 9. dry 10. waters
11. True 12. True 13. False 14. True 15. True
16. B 17. C 18. D 19. E 20. A
SUMMARY
Pupils learned that the crossing of the Red Sea was a great event in which God made a way for the Israelites to escape from the Egyptian army. Moses stretched his staff over the sea, and the waters were divided so that the Israelites could cross on dry ground.
Pupils also learned that the Egyptian army followed the Israelites into the sea, but the waters returned and covered the Egyptians. The event teaches us to trust God, obey His instructions and remain courageous during difficult situations.
PRESENTATION
To deliver the lesson, the teacher adopts the following steps:
Step 1: Introduction
The teacher asks pupils:
- What happened after Pharaoh allowed the Israelites to leave Egypt?
- What would you do if you were trapped between danger and a large body of water?
- Who do you think could help the Israelites?
The teacher introduces the lesson by explaining that God helped the Israelites when they were trapped at the Red Sea.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils answer the questions and share what they know about the Israelites’ journey from Egypt.
Step 2: Meaning of the Crossing of the Red Sea
The teacher explains that the crossing of the Red Sea refers to the miraculous event in which God made a way for the Israelites to cross the sea and escape from the Egyptian army.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils listen and explain the meaning of the crossing of the Red Sea.
Step 3: The Israelites at the Red Sea
The teacher explains that Pharaoh sent his army after the Israelites. The Israelites reached the Red Sea and became afraid when they saw the Egyptian army approaching.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils describe the situation of the Israelites at the Red Sea.
Step 4: The Miracle at the Red Sea
The teacher explains that God instructed Moses to stretch his staff over the sea. A strong wind blew, and the waters were divided. The Israelites crossed on dry ground.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils listen to the story and explain how the Israelites crossed the sea.
Step 5: The Destruction of the Egyptians
The teacher explains that the Egyptian army followed the Israelites into the sea. After the Israelites had crossed safely, Moses stretched his hand over the sea again, and the waters returned and covered the Egyptian army.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils explain what happened to the Egyptian army.
Step 6: Lessons from the Crossing
The teacher explains that the event teaches us to trust God, obey His instructions, remain courageous and believe that God can save His people from danger.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils state lessons they have learned from the crossing of the Red Sea.
Step 7: Group Activity
The teacher divides pupils into four groups:
- Group 1: Explain the meaning of the crossing of the Red Sea.
- Group 2: Narrate five important events in the crossing of the Red Sea.
- Group 3: Explain what happened to the Egyptian army.
- Group 4: State four lessons from the crossing of the Red Sea.
The teacher guides the groups and allows each group to present its answers.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils discuss, write and present their answers to the class.
Step 8: Lesson Summary and Evaluation
The teacher reviews the meaning and story of the crossing of the Red Sea and the destruction of the Egyptian army. The teacher gives pupils a different set of 20 questions to assess their understanding of the lesson.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils answer the questions individually or in groups and summarise what they have learned.
CONCLUSION
To conclude the lesson for the week, the teacher revises the entire lesson and links it to the following week’s lesson.
NEXT LESSON
Entry into the Promised Land: Meaning of Entry, Crossing the River Jordan, and the Joy of Crossing the River Jordan | Primary 6 (Basic 6) First Term Week 6 Christian Religious Studies
LESSON EVALUATION
Teacher asks pupils,
1. What is the crossing of the Red Sea?
2. Why did the Israelites become afraid at the Red Sea?
3. How did God help the Israelites cross the Red Sea?
4. What happened to the Egyptian army?
5. State four lessons from the crossing of the Red Sea.

topics.title: Entry into the Promised Land: Meaning of Entry, Crossing the River Jordan, and the Joy of Crossing the River Jordan | Primary 6 (Basic 6) First Term Week 6 Christian Religious Studies
topics.content:
ENTRY INTO THE PROMISED LAND: MEANING OF ENTRY, CROSSING THE RIVER JORDAN, AND THE JOY OF CROSSING THE RIVER JORDAN
CHRISTIAN RELIGIOUS STUDIES (CRS)
PRIMARY 6 - FIRST TERM - WEEK 6
THEME - NATIONAL RELIGIOUS STUDIES
PREVIOUS LESSON - The Crossing of the Red Sea: Meaning and Story of the Crossing, and the Destruction of the Egyptians | Primary 6 (Basic 6) First Term Week 5 Christian Religious Studies
TOPIC - ENTRY INTO THE PROMISED LAND
LEARNING AREA
1. Introduction
2. Meaning of Entry
3. Crossing the River Jordan
4. The Joy of Crossing the River Jordan
5. Lessons from the Entry into the Promised Land
6. Weekly Assessment: Test Questions and Answers/Assignment
7. Summary
LEARNING OBJECTIVES
By the end of the lesson, pupils should be able to:
1. Explain the meaning of entry.
2. Describe how the Israelites crossed the River Jordan.
3. Explain the role of Joshua in the crossing of the River Jordan.
4. Describe the joy of the Israelites after crossing the River Jordan.
5. State lessons from the entry into the Promised Land.
ENTRY BEHAVIOUR
Pupils have learned about the crossing of the Red Sea and how God delivered the Israelites from the Egyptians.
This lesson builds on that knowledge by teaching pupils how God helped the Israelites cross the River Jordan and enter the Promised Land.
INSTRUCTIONAL MATERIALS
The teacher will teach the lesson with the aid of:
1. Holy Bible and story illustrations
2. Pictures of Joshua and the Israelites
3. Map showing the River Jordan and Canaan
4. Charts
5. Flashcards
6. Story illustrations
METHOD OF TEACHING
The teacher uses questioning, storytelling, explanation, discussion and demonstration.
The teacher begins with questions about reaching a long-awaited destination to arouse pupils’ interest.
REFERENCE MATERIALS
1. Scheme of Work
2. 9-Year Basic Education Curriculum
3. CRS Course Book
4. Holy Bible - Joshua 3:1-17; Joshua 4:1-24
5. Relevant teaching materials
6. Online information
CONTENT OF THE LESSON
INTRODUCTION
After wandering in the wilderness for many years, the Israelites came close to the Promised Land. Moses had died, and Joshua became their leader.
God instructed Joshua to lead the Israelites across the River Jordan and into the land He had promised to give them.
The crossing of the Jordan showed that God continued to guide and help His people.
LESSON 1 - MEANING OF ENTRY
Entry means the act of going into or arriving at a place.
The entry of the Israelites into the Promised Land means their arrival in the land God had promised to give them.
The Promised Land refers to the land of Canaan that God promised to Abraham and his descendants.
CROSSING THE RIVER JORDAN
Joshua led the Israelites to the River Jordan. At that time, the river was overflowing its banks.
The priests carrying the Ark of the Covenant went ahead of the people.
God instructed the priests to step into the River Jordan. As soon as their feet touched the water, the flowing water stopped, and the river became dry.
The priests stood in the middle of the river while all the Israelites crossed over on dry ground.
After everyone had crossed, God instructed Joshua to choose twelve men, one from each tribe, to take twelve stones from the middle of the river.
The stones were taken to the place where the Israelites camped as a reminder of what God had done for them.
When the priests came out of the river, the water returned to its normal flow.
LESSON 2 - THE JOY OF CROSSING THE RIVER JORDAN
The Israelites were happy and thankful after crossing the River Jordan safely.
They were joyful because God had helped them enter the land He had promised them.
The twelve stones served as a reminder to future generations of how God stopped the River Jordan and brought the Israelites safely into the Promised Land.
The event strengthened their faith in God and encouraged them to trust Him.
LESSON 3 - LESSONS FROM THE ENTRY INTO THE PROMISED LAND
The crossing of the River Jordan teaches us that:
1. We should trust God in difficult situations.
2. We should obey God’s instructions.
3. God keeps His promises.
4. We should be thankful for God’s help.
5. We should remember and tell others about God’s goodness.
6. Good leaders should guide people with faith and courage.
7. We should not give up when facing challenges.
WEEKLY ASSESSMENT: TEST QUESTIONS AND ANSWERS/ASSIGNMENT
A. Multiple Choice Questions
1. What does entry mean?
A. The act of leaving a place
B. The act of sleeping
C. The act of going into a place
D. The act of travelling by air
2. Who led the Israelites into the Promised Land?
A. Caleb
B. Aaron
C. Joshua
D. Moses
3. Which river did the Israelites cross?
A. River Nile
B. River Jordan
C. River Euphrates
D. River Niger
4. What happened when the priests carrying the Ark stepped into the Jordan?
A. The river became deeper
B. The river flooded the people
C. The priests returned to camp
D. The river stopped flowing
5. How did the Israelites cross the River Jordan?
A. On dry ground
B. By boats
C. By swimming
D. On horses
B. Fill in the Gaps
6. Joshua led the Israelites into the ______ Land.
7. The Israelites crossed the River ______.
8. The priests carried the Ark of the ______.
9. The Israelites crossed the river on ______ ground.
10. Joshua chose ______ men to take twelve stones from the river.
C. True or False
16. Joshua became the leader of the Israelites after Moses died.
17. The River Jordan was flowing normally when the Israelites crossed it.
18. The priests carrying the Ark went ahead of the people.
19. The Israelites crossed the River Jordan on dry ground.
20. The twelve stones were used as a reminder of God’s miracle.
D. Matching
16. Joshua - A. Carried the Ark of the Covenant
17. Twelve stones - B. Leader of the Israelites
18. Promised Land - C. River crossed by the Israelites
19. Priests - D. Reminder of God’s miracle
20. River Jordan - E. Land of Canaan
ANSWER KEY
1. C 2. D 3. B 4. D 5. A
6. Promised 7. Jordan 8. Covenant 9. dry 10. twelve
11. True 12. False. 13. True. 14. True 15. True
16. B 17. D 18. E 19. A 20. C
SUMMARY
Pupils learned that entry means the act of going into or arriving at a place. The Israelites entered the Promised Land under the leadership of Joshua after crossing the River Jordan.
Pupils also learned that God stopped the flow of the River Jordan so that the Israelites could cross on dry ground. They were joyful and thankful because God had fulfilled His promise and safely brought them into the Promised Land.
PRESENTATION
To deliver the lesson, the teacher adopts the following steps:
Step 1: Introduction
The teacher asks pupils:
- What does it mean to enter a place?
- How would you feel if you finally reached a place you had been waiting for?
- What happened to the Israelites after Moses died?
The teacher introduces the lesson by explaining that Joshua led the Israelites towards the Promised Land.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils answer the questions and share what they know about entering a new place.
Step 2: Meaning of Entry
The teacher explains that entry means the act of going into or arriving at a place. The teacher explains that the Israelites’ entry into the Promised Land meant their arrival in Canaan, the land God had promised them.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils listen and explain the meaning of entry in their own words.
Step 3: Crossing the River Jordan
The teacher explains that Joshua led the Israelites to the River Jordan. The priests carrying the Ark of the Covenant went ahead of the people.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils listen and mention who led the Israelites and what the priests carried.
Step 4: The Miracle at the River Jordan
The teacher explains that when the priests stepped into the river, the flowing water stopped. The priests stood in the middle of the river while the Israelites crossed on dry ground.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils describe what happened to the River Jordan.
Step 5: The Twelve Stones
The teacher explains that Joshua chose twelve men, one from each tribe, to take twelve stones from the middle of the river. The stones were kept as a reminder of God’s miracle.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils explain why the twelve stones were important.
Step 6: The Joy of Crossing the River Jordan
The teacher explains that the Israelites were happy and thankful after crossing the river safely. They were joyful because God had fulfilled His promise and helped them enter the Promised Land.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils mention reasons why the Israelites were joyful and thankful.
Step 7: Group Activity
The teacher divides pupils into four groups:
- Group 1: Explain the meaning of entry and the Promised Land.
- Group 2: Describe how the Israelites crossed the River Jordan.
- Group 3: Explain the importance of the twelve stones.
- Group 4: State four lessons from the crossing of the River Jordan.
The teacher guides the groups and allows each group to present its answers.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils discuss, write and present their answers to the class.
Step 8: Lesson Summary and Evaluation
The teacher reviews the meaning of entry, the crossing of the River Jordan, the twelve stones and the joy of the Israelites. The teacher gives pupils a different set of 20 questions to assess their understanding of the lesson.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils answer the questions individually or in groups and summarise what they have learned.
CONCLUSION
To conclude the lesson for the week, the teacher revises the entire lesson and links it to the following week’s lesson.
NEXT LESSON
The Twelve Stones: Meaning and Importance of the Twelve Stones Placed at the River Jordan | Primary 6 (Basic 6) First Term Week 8 Christian Religious Studies
LESSON EVALUATION
Teacher asks pupils,
1. What is the meaning of entry?
2. Who led the Israelites into the Promised Land?
3. Which river did the Israelites cross?
4. How did the Israelites cross the River Jordan?
5. Why were the Israelites joyful after crossing the river?

topics.title: The Twelve Stones: Meaning and Importance of the Twelve Stones Placed at the River Jordan | Primary 6 (Basic 6) First Term Week 8 Christian Religious Studies
topics.content:
THE TWELVE STONES: MEANING AND IMPORTANCE OF TWELVE STONES AT THE RIVER JORDAN
CHRISTIAN RELIGIOUS STUDIES (CRS)
PRIMARY 6 - FIRST TERM - WEEK 8
THEME - NATIONAL RELIGIOUS STUDIES
PREVIOUS LESSON - Entry into the Promised Land: Meaning of Entry, Crossing the River Jordan, and the Joy of Crossing the River Jordan | Primary 6 (Basic 6) First Term Week 6 Christian Religious Studies
TOPIC - THE TWELVE STONES
LEARNING AREA
1. Introduction
2. Meaning of the Twelve Stones
3. How the Twelve Stones Were Collected
4. Importance of the Twelve Stones
5. Lessons from the Twelve Stones
6. Weekly Assessment: Test Questions and Answers/Assignment
7. Summary
LEARNING OBJECTIVES
By the end of the lesson, pupils should be able to:
1. Explain the meaning of the twelve stones.
2. Describe how the twelve stones were collected from the River Jordan.
3. Explain why Joshua instructed the Israelites to collect the stones.
4. State the importance of the twelve stones.
5. State lessons Christians can learn from the twelve stones.
ENTRY BEHAVIOUR
Pupils have learned how the Israelites crossed the River Jordan on dry ground under the leadership of Joshua.
This lesson builds on that knowledge by teaching pupils about the twelve stones taken from the River Jordan as a reminder of God’s mighty work.
INSTRUCTIONAL MATERIALS
The teacher will teach the lesson with the aid of:
1. Holy Bible and story illustrations
2. Pictures of Joshua and the Israelites
3. Pictures or samples of stones
4. Map showing the River Jordan
5. Charts
6. Flashcards
METHOD OF TEACHING
The teacher uses questioning, storytelling, explanation, discussion and demonstration.
The teacher begins with questions about how people remember important events to arouse pupils’ interest.
REFERENCE MATERIALS
1. Scheme of Work
2. 9-Year Basic Education Curriculum
3. CRS Course Book
4. Holy Bible - Joshua 4:1-24
5. Relevant teaching materials
6. Online information
CONTENT OF THE LESSON
INTRODUCTION
After the Israelites crossed the River Jordan safely, God instructed Joshua to choose twelve men from among the people.
One man was chosen from each of the twelve tribes of Israel. Each man was to take one stone from the middle of the River Jordan.
The stones were carried to the Israelites’ camp and set up as a reminder of how God had helped His people cross the river.
LESSON 1 - MEANING OF THE TWELVE STONES
The twelve stones were stones taken from the middle of the River Jordan by twelve Israelites.
Each of the twelve men represented one of the twelve tribes of Israel.
The stones were set up as a memorial. A memorial is something kept or created to help people remember an important event or person.
The twelve stones reminded the Israelites of how God stopped the flow of the River Jordan and helped them cross safely.
HOW THE TWELVE STONES WERE COLLECTED
After all the Israelites had crossed the River Jordan, God instructed Joshua to choose twelve men.
Each man took one stone from the place where the priests carrying the Ark of the Covenant had stood.
The twelve men carried the stones to the camp where the Israelites stayed.
Joshua arranged for the stones to be set up as a memorial.
The stones helped the Israelites remember what God had done for them.
LESSON 2 - IMPORTANCE OF THE TWELVE STONES
The twelve stones were important because:
1. They served as a memorial: They helped the Israelites remember God’s mighty work.
2. They showed God’s power: They reminded the people that God stopped the flow of the Jordan River.
3. They strengthened faith: Remembering God’s help encouraged the Israelites to trust Him.
4. They taught future generations: Parents could explain to their children what God had done.
5. They showed God’s faithfulness: The stones reminded the Israelites that God fulfilled His promise to bring them into the Promised Land.
6. They encouraged thanksgiving: The Israelites could remember God’s goodness and give thanks to Him.
LESSON 3 - LESSONS FROM THE TWELVE STONES
The twelve stones teach us that:
1. We should remember God’s goodness.
2. We should always be thankful for God’s help.
3. We should trust God in difficult situations.
4. We should tell others about the good things God has done.
5. Parents and teachers should teach children about God’s works.
6. We should remember important lessons from the past.
7. God is faithful and keeps His promises.
WEEKLY ASSESSMENT: TEST QUESTIONS AND ANSWERS/ASSIGNMENT
A. Multiple Choice Questions
1. Where were the twelve stones taken from?
A. River Jordan
B. Red Sea
C. River Nile
D. River Niger
2. Who instructed the Israelites to collect the twelve stones?
A. Moses
B. Aaron
C. Caleb
D. Joshua
3. How many men were chosen to collect the stones?
A. Seven
B. Ten
C. Forty
D. Twelve
4. What did the twelve stones serve as?
A. A memorial
B. A weapon
C. A bridge
D. A house
5. What did the stones remind the Israelites about?
A. Their journey to Egypt
B. How God helped them cross the Jordan
C. The birth of Moses
D. The building of Jerusalem
B. Fill in the Gaps
6. The twelve stones were taken from the River _____.
7. _____ instructed the Israelites to collect the stones.
8. One man was chosen from each of the _____ tribes.
9. The stones served as a _____ of God’s mighty work.
10. The stones helped future generations remember God’s _____.
C. True or False
11. The twelve stones were taken from the River Nile.
12. Joshua instructed twelve men to collect the stones.
13. The stones helped the Israelites remember God’s help.
14. Christians should remember and be thankful for God’s goodness.
15. The stones were collected to build houses.
D. Matching
16. Joshua - A. Twelve
17. Twelve Stones - B. Memorial
18. Promised Land - C. Leader of Israel
19. Twelve tribes - D. Land of Canaan
20. River Jordan - E. River crossed by the Israelites
ANSWER KEY
1. C 2. D 3. D 4. A. 5. B
6. Jordan 7. Joshua 8. twelve 9. memorial 10. goodness
11. True 12. True 13. True 14. True 15. False
16. C 17. B 18. D 19. A 20. E
SUMMARY
Pupils learned that the twelve stones were taken from the middle of the River Jordan after the Israelites crossed the river. Joshua chose twelve men, one from each tribe, to collect the stones.
Pupils also learned that the stones served as a memorial of God’s mighty work. They reminded the Israelites and future generations of God’s power, faithfulness, protection and help.
PRESENTATION
To deliver the lesson, the teacher adopts the following steps:
Step 1: Introduction
The teacher asks pupils:
- How can we remember an important event?
- Why do people keep things as reminders?
- What happened after the Israelites crossed the River Jordan?
The teacher introduces the lesson by explaining that the Israelites collected twelve stones after crossing the River Jordan.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils answer the questions and share what they know about remembering important events.
Step 2: Meaning of the Twelve Stones
The teacher explains that the twelve stones were taken from the middle of the River Jordan by twelve men, one from each tribe of Israel.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils listen and explain the meaning of the twelve stones in their own words.
Step 3: How the Stones Were Collected
The teacher explains that Joshua chose twelve men to take stones from the place where the priests carrying the Ark of the Covenant had stood.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils listen and state how the stones were collected.
Step 4: Purpose of the Stones
The teacher explains that the stones were set up as a memorial to remind the Israelites of how God helped them cross the River Jordan.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils explain why the stones were kept as a memorial.
Step 5: Importance of the Twelve Stones
The teacher explains that the stones reminded the Israelites of God’s power, faithfulness, protection and help.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils mention the importance of the twelve stones.
Step 6: Lessons from the Twelve Stones
The teacher explains that Christians should remember God’s goodness, trust Him, teach children about His works and give thanks for His help.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils state lessons they have learned from the twelve stones.
Step 7: Group Activity
The teacher divides pupils into four groups:
- Group 1: Explain the meaning of the twelve stones.
- Group 2: Describe how the twelve stones were collected.
- Group 3: State four importance of the twelve stones.
- Group 4: State four lessons Christians can learn from the twelve stones.
The teacher guides the groups and allows each group to present its answers.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils discuss, write and present their answers to the class.
Step 8: Lesson Summary and Evaluation
The teacher reviews the meaning, collection, importance and lessons of the twelve stones. The teacher gives pupils a different set of 20 questions to assess their understanding of the lesson.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils answer the questions individually or in groups and summarise what they have learned.
CONCLUSION
To conclude the lesson for the week, the teacher revises the entire lesson and links it to the following week’s lesson.
NEXT LESSON

Teacher asks pupils,
1. What were the twelve stones?
2. Where were the twelve stones taken from?
3. Who instructed the Israelites to collect the stones?
4. State three importance of the twelve stones.
5. Mention three lessons Christians can learn from the twelve stones.

topics.content:
THE TWELVE TRIBES OF ISRAEL: MEANING, NAMES AND DISCUSSION OF THE TWELVE TRIBES OF ISRAEL
CHRISTIAN RELIGIOUS STUDIES (CRS)
PRIMARY 6 - FIRST TERM - WEEK 9
THEME - NATIONAL RELIGIOUS STUDIES
PREVIOUS LESSON - The Twelve Stones: Meaning and Importance of the Twelve Stones Placed at the River Jordan | Primary 6 (Basic 6) First Term Week 8 Christian Religious Studies
TOPIC - THE TWELVE TRIBES OF ISRAEL
LEARNING AREA
1. Introduction
2. Meaning of the Twelve Tribes of Israel
3. Names of the Twelve Tribes of Israel
4. Lessons from the Twelve Tribes of Israel
5. Weekly Assessment: Test Questions and Answers/Assignment
6. Summary
LEARNING OBJECTIVES
By the end of the lesson, pupils should be able to:
1. Explain the meaning of the twelve tribes of Israel.
2. Name the twelve tribes of Israel.
3. Explain the origin of the twelve tribes.
4. Discuss some important facts about the twelve tribes.
5. State lessons Christians can learn from the twelve tribes of Israel.
ENTRY BEHAVIOUR
Pupils have learned about the twelve stones taken from the River Jordan and the twelve tribes of Israel represented by the twelve men who collected the stones.
This lesson builds on that knowledge by teaching pupils about the meaning, names and background of the twelve tribes of Israel.
INSTRUCTIONAL MATERIALS
The teacher will teach the lesson with the aid of:
1. Holy Bible and story illustrations
2. Chart showing the twelve tribes
3. Pictures of Jacob and his sons
4. Map of ancient Israel
5. Flashcards
METHOD OF TEACHING
The teacher uses questioning, storytelling, explanation, discussion and demonstration.
The teacher begins with questions about families and groups to introduce the idea of tribes.
REFERENCE MATERIALS
1. Scheme of Work
2. 9-Year Basic Education Curriculum
3. CRS Course Book
4. Holy Bible - Genesis 35:22-26; Genesis 49:1-28
5. Relevant teaching materials
6. Online information
CONTENT OF THE LESSON
INTRODUCTION
The nation of Israel came from Jacob, whom God later named Israel.
Jacob had twelve sons. Their descendants became the twelve tribes of Israel.
The twelve tribes played an important role in the history of God’s people. The tribes formed the family groups that made up the nation of Israel.
LESSON 1 AND LESSON 2 - MEANING OF THE TWELVE TRIBES OF ISRAEL
A tribe is a large group of people who are related by family or ancestry.
The twelve tribes of Israel were the twelve major family groups that came from the descendants of Jacob’s twelve sons.
Jacob was also called Israel. His twelve sons became the ancestors of the twelve tribes.
The twelve tribes formed the people of Israel and later received different areas of land in the Promised Land.
NAMES OF THE TWELVE TRIBES OF ISRAEL
The twelve sons of Jacob were:
1. Ruben - Reuben was Jacob’s firstborn son. His descendants formed the tribe of Reuben.
2. Simeon - Simeon was Jacob’s second son. His descendants became the tribe of Simeon.
3. Levi - Levi was Jacob’s third son. The descendants of Levi were chosen for special duties connected with worship and the tabernacle.
4. Judah - Judah was one of Jacob’s sons. The tribe of Judah became an important tribe in Israel’s history. King David came from Judah.
5. Dan - Dan was one of Jacob’s sons. His descendants formed the tribe of Dan.
6. Naphtali - Naphtali was one of Jacob’s sons. His descendants became the tribe of Naphtali.
7. Gad - Gad was one of Jacob’s sons. His descendants formed the tribe of Gad.
8. Asher - Asher was one of Jacob’s sons. His descendants became the tribe of Asher.
9. Issachar - Issachar was one of Jacob’s sons. His descendants formed the tribe of Issachar.
10. Zebulun - Zebulun was one of Jacob’s sons. His descendants became the tribe of Zebulun.
11. Joseph - Joseph was one of Jacob’s sons. He became a powerful leader in Egypt and had two sons, Ephraim and Manasseh.
12. Benjamin - Benjamin was Jacob’s youngest son. His descendants formed the tribe of Benjamin.
These names are commonly used to identify the twelve sons of Jacob and the tribes that came from them.
Important Note
In some biblical lists, the names of the tribes differ because the tribe of Levi was set apart for priestly service, while Joseph’s descendants were represented by his two sons, Ephraim and Manasseh.
For this reason, different passages may list the tribes differently depending on the purpose of the list.
LESSON 3 - IMPORTANCE OF THE TWELVE TRIBES
The twelve tribes were important because:
1. They formed the nation of Israel.
2. They came from the family of Jacob.
3. They received different portions of the Promised Land.
4. They helped preserve the identity of God’s people.
5. They played different roles in the history of Israel.
6. They remind us of God’s promise to Abraham, Isaac and Jacob.
LESSONS FROM THE TWELVE TRIBES OF ISRAEL
The twelve tribes teach us that:
1. Family relationships are important.
2. God keeps His promises.
3. People can have different roles and responsibilities.
4. We should work together despite our differences.
5. We should respect one another.
6. We should value our identity and heritage.
7. We should remain faithful to God.
WEEKLY ASSESSMENT: TEST QUESTIONS AND ANSWERS/ASSIGNMENT
A. Multiple Choice Questions
1. Who was the father of the twelve sons from whom the tribes of Israel came?
A. Moses
B. Jacob
C. Joshua
D. Aaron
2. What was Jacob also called?
A. Israel
B. Judah
C. Joseph
D. Benjamin
3. How many major tribes came from Jacob’s sons?
A. Seven
B. Ten
C. Twelve
D. Fourteen
4. Which of Jacob’s sons was the youngest?
A. Joseph
B. Benjamin
C. Judah
D. Reuben
5. Which tribe was set apart for special duties connected with worship?
A. Levi
B. Dan
C. Gad
D. Asher
B. Fill in the Gaps
6. Jacob was also called ______.
7. The twelve tribes came from the twelve ______ of Jacob.
8. ______ was Jacob’s firstborn son.
9. Joseph had two sons called Ephraim and ______.
10. The tribe of ______ was associated with special duties of worship.
C. True or False
11. Jacob had twelve sons.
12. Jacob was also called Israel.
13. Benjamin was Jacob’s oldest son.
14. The tribe of Levi was associated with special duties connected with worship.
15. The twelve tribes formed an important part of the nation of Israel.
D. Matching
16. Benjamin - A. Youngest son
17. Reuben - B. Also called Israel
18. Levi - C. Firstborn son
19. Joseph - D. Special worship duties
20. Jacob - E. Father of Ephraim and Manasseh
ANSWER KEY
1. B 2. A 3. C 4. B 5. A
6. Israel 7. sons 8. Reuben 9. Manasseh 10. Levi
11. True 12. True 13. False 14. True 15. True
16. A 17. C 18. D 19. E 20. B
SUMMARY
Pupils learned that the twelve tribes of Israel came from the twelve sons of Jacob. Jacob was also called Israel, and his descendants became the people who formed the nation of Israel.
Pupils also learned the names of the twelve sons and some important facts about the tribes. They learned that the tribes had different roles and responsibilities but were all part of God’s people.
PRESENTATION
To deliver the lesson, the teacher adopts the following steps:
Step 1: Introduction
The teacher asks pupils:
- What is a family?
- What is a tribe?
- Who was Jacob?
- What was Jacob also called?
The teacher introduces the lesson by explaining that Jacob’s descendants became the twelve tribes of Israel.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils answer the questions and share what they know about families and tribes.
Step 2: Meaning of the Twelve Tribes of Israel
The teacher explains that the twelve tribes of Israel were the major family groups that came from the descendants of Jacob’s twelve sons.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils listen and explain the meaning of the twelve tribes in their own words.
Step 3: Names of the Twelve Tribes
The teacher displays a chart and introduces the names of Jacob’s twelve sons: Reuben, Simeon, Levi, Judah, Dan, Naphtali, Gad, Asher, Issachar, Zebulun, Joseph and Benjamin.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils read and repeat the names of the twelve tribes.
Step 4: Discussion of the Tribes
The teacher discusses some important facts about the tribes, including Reuben as the firstborn, Benjamin as the youngest, Levi’s special worship duties, Judah’s importance in Israel’s history and Joseph’s two sons, Ephraim and Manasseh.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils listen and mention facts about the tribes.
Step 5: Importance of the Twelve Tribes
The teacher explains that the tribes formed the nation of Israel and helped preserve the identity and history of God’s people.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils state the importance of the twelve tribes.
Step 6: Lessons from the Twelve Tribes
The teacher explains that people may have different roles but should respect one another, work together and remain faithful to God.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils state lessons they have learned from the twelve tribes.
Step 7: Group Activity
The teacher divides pupils into four groups:
- Group 1: Explain the meaning of the twelve tribes of Israel.
- Group 2: List the twelve sons of Jacob.
- Group 3: Discuss four important facts about the twelve tribes.
- Group 4: State four lessons Christians can learn from the twelve tribes.
The teacher guides the groups and allows each group to present its answers.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils discuss, write and present their answers to the class.
Step 8: Lesson Summary and Evaluation
The teacher reviews the meaning, names, importance and lessons of the twelve tribes of Israel. The teacher gives pupils a different set of 20 questions to assess their understanding of the lesson.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils answer the questions individually or in groups and summarise what they have learned.
CONCLUSION
To conclude the lesson for the week, the teacher revises the entire lesson and links it to the following week’s lesson.
NEXT LESSON
LESSON EVALUATION
Teacher asks pupils,
1. What is a tribe?
2. Who was the father of the twelve sons of Israel?
3. Name the twelve sons of Jacob.
4. State three importance of the twelve tribes of Israel.
5. Mention three lessons Christians can learn from the twelve tribes.
